hub_tagline: Five meanings of "finished". They nest inside each other, and each has a term that sits in it but not in the next.

concepts.title: Concept: βη-Normal Form
concepts.tagline: No β-redex and no η-redex anywhere. The strictest notion of finished.
concepts.sentence: A term is in βη-normal form when it contains neither (λx. M) N nor λx. M x (x ∉ FV(M)) anywhere, even under λ.
concepts.analogy_big: A fully simplified fraction: nothing cancels and nothing can be rewritten shorter.
concepts.analogy: Not even a forwarding wrapper is left.
concepts.see:
f                               ✓     ✓    ✓     ✓    ✓
λx. f x                         ·     ✓    ✓     ✓    ✓

Real demo output (columns: βη-NF, β-NF, HNF, WHNF, value). λx. f x is β-normal but not βη-normal: it's an η-redex.
concepts.wrong: "β-normal and βη-normal are the same thing."
concepts.right: They differ exactly by η. λx. f x is β-normal, and η-reduces to f. βη-NF is where two extensionally equal functions become syntactically equal.
concepts.connects: Every βη-normal form is a β-normal form, which is a head normal form, which is a WHNF.

concepts.title: Concept: β-Normal Form
concepts.tagline: No β-redex anywhere, including under λ. What normal order produces.
concepts.sentence: A term is in β-normal form when no sub-term has the shape (λx. M) N. It's what "the normal form" means by default.
concepts.analogy_big: Every envelope in the pile has been opened, even the ones tucked inside folders.
concepts.analogy: Whatever is left can't compute any further.
concepts.see:
x ((λa. a) b)                   ·     ·    ✓     ✓    ·

Head normal, but not β-normal: a redex remains inside the argument.
concepts.wrong: "If a term's head is a variable, it's in normal form."
concepts.right: That's head normal form. β-normal form also requires that the arguments (and everything under every λ) be redex-free.
concepts.connects: Stricter: βη-normal form. Looser: head normal form. Unique when it exists, by Church–Rosser (Module 10).

concepts.title: Concept: Head Normal Form
concepts.tagline: λx1…xn. y M1 … Mk: a variable sits at the head. Arguments may still compute.
concepts.sentence: A term is in head normal form (HNF) when, after its leading λs, its head is a variable. Nothing can ever change that outline, whatever happens in the arguments.
concepts.analogy_big: The headline of a newspaper is printed. The articles below may still be edited.
concepts.analogy: Whatever edits happen, the front page's headline is final.
concepts.see:
x ((λa. a) b)                   ·     ·    ✓     ✓    ·
λx. (λy. y) x                   ·     ·    ·     ✓    ✓

The first is HNF (head x). The second is not: under its λ, the head is a redex.
concepts.wrong: "HNF and WHNF differ only in the word 'weak'."
concepts.right: HNF looks under the leading λs, and WHNF doesn't. λx. (λy. y) x is WHNF (it starts with λ) but not HNF (under that λ the head is a redex).
concepts.connects: Between β-normal form (stricter) and WHNF (looser). Terms with no HNF (like λx. Ω) are called unsolvable, the λ-calculus's notion of "meaningless".

concepts.title: Concept: Weak Head Normal Form
concepts.tagline: A λ, or a variable applied to arguments. Where lazy evaluation stops.
concepts.sentence: A term is in weak head normal form (WHNF) when it is an abstraction λx. M (anything inside) or a neutral term y M1 … Mk.
concepts.analogy_big: A wrapped present: you know it's a present, and you haven't opened it.
concepts.analogy: Lazy languages stop here until someone actually needs what's inside.
concepts.see:
to WHNF (call-by-name)             λy. (λz. (λw. w) z) y        1 step(s)
to HNF (head reduction)            λy. y                        3 step(s)

Real demo output: call-by-name stops as soon as the term is a λ.
concepts.wrong: "A term in WHNF has finished computing."
concepts.right: WHNF only fixes the outer shape. λx. Ω is in WHNF, yet running its body never finishes. Haskell's seq evaluates to exactly this form.
concepts.connects: The loosest form in the chain: HNF ⊆ WHNF. Every value is in WHNF.

concepts.title: Concept: Value
concepts.tagline: In call-by-value, a λ or a variable: something that may be passed as an argument.
concepts.sentence: A value is what call-by-value is allowed to substitute: an abstraction or (for open terms) a variable. (λx. M) V → M[x := V] requires V to be a value.
concepts.analogy_big: A value is a sealed package the post office will accept.
concepts.analogy: Loose, still-changing contents must be packed (evaluated) before they can be sent.
concepts.see:
λx. (λy. y y) (λy. y y)         ·     ·    ·     ✓    ✓

λx. Ω is a value, and head reduction on it runs out of fuel.
concepts.wrong: "A value is a term in normal form."
concepts.right: A value may contain redexes under its λ (λx. (λy. y) x), and a normal form need not be a value (x y is normal but not a value).
concepts.connects: Values ⊆ WHNF. A value is independent of β-normal form: neither implies the other.

pairs: "λx. (λy. y) x is in head normal form: it starts with λ."
Starting with λ gives WHNF. HNF looks under the λ, where the head is a redex.
"It's in WHNF, so evaluation is done."
Only the outer shape is fixed. λx. Ω is WHNF with an infinite body.
λx. (λy. y) x is a value, not normal. x y is normal, not a value.
Arguments may still hold redexes: x ((λa. a) b).
quiz: λx. f x, the tightest form it is in.
No β-redex, but it is an η-redex, so not βη-normal.
Its head is the variable x, but a redex hides in the argument.
λx. (λy. y) x, the tightest of HNF / WHNF.
It starts with λ, but under it the head is a redex.
What call-by-value may pass into (λx. M) □.
What Haskell's seq forces its first argument to.
Just enough to know the outer constructor or λ.
